source: Simon, Pham, Le & Holyoak (2001) The emergence of coherence over the course of decision making
finding: Students read an ambiguous libel case (Quest v. Smith) and rated six disputed arguments before the case, after reading it, and after the verdict. Ratings spread apart toward the eventual verdict already at the interim test, before any commitment was recorded (Exp 1, delay instructions).
numbers: Exp 1: 50 UCLA undergraduates, 47 analysed (3 switchers dropped). Verdicts 49% Quest, 51% Smith; 93% at least moderately confident. Baseline gap between eventual Quest and Smith supporters 0.80; interim gap 2.23; postdecision gap 2.55. Verdict x test interaction F(2,86)=35.3, p<.0001. Interim to postdecision change not significant (p>.30).
limits: One case, one student population, one rating scale. Coherence is measured on the same arguments the person later uses to decide, so the spread is partly the decision forming.
agent_relevance: In an agent the weights it gives to evidence will drift toward its leading answer while it reads. That drift is invisible unless the pre-read ratings were logged by code.

source: Simon, Pham, Le & Holyoak (2001) The emergence of coherence over the course of decision making
finding: The jump in internal consistency of the ratings is large. Before the case the six arguments and the verdict are nearly uncorrelated. After reading, nearly all are positively correlated.
numbers: Exp 1: Cronbach alpha across the six points -0.25 at baseline, 0.74 interim, 0.80 postdecision. Only 2 of 21 correlations significantly positive at baseline; all but 5 positive at interim.
limits: Alpha is computed within the same people who then pick a side; it shows coherence, not accuracy. Coherent and wrong looks identical.
agent_relevance: Coherence of the agent's own evidence ratings is cheap to compute in code and rises on its own; a high value must not be read as a sign the answer is right (G3, G4).

source: Simon, Pham, Le & Holyoak (2001) The emergence of coherence over the course of decision making
finding: Coherence shift does not need a decision. It appeared when students were told only to memorize the case (Exp 2) and when told only to comprehend it (Exp 3).
numbers: Exp 2: 125 students, 120 analysed; verdicts 44% for one side; interaction F(2,236)=59.1, p<.0001; alpha 0.08 baseline, 0.70 interim, 0.80 postdecision. Exp 3: 166 students, 157 analysed; three sets (decision, reception, communication) did not differ, F(4,302)<1; interaction F(2,302)=78.6; alpha 0.12, 0.77, 0.80.
limits: Same single case in all three experiments. Memorize and comprehend sets still involve reading a conflict-laden text, which may invite a leaning anyway.
agent_relevance: Shows the pull toward one coherent reading is a by-product of processing, not a choice. A scaffold cannot avoid it by saying 'do not decide yet'; it must freeze ratings before reading (S2 record).

source: Holyoak & Simon (1999) Bidirectional reasoning in decision making by constraint satisfaction (JEP General 128(1), 3-31)
finding: Founding experiment for coherence shift in a legal case. Ratings of individual arguments moved toward the verdict, and the main shift came before the verdict was reported (3-phase condition).
numbers: Exp 1: 54 students (24 in 2-phase, 30 in 3-phase); 6 of 30 3-phase participants switched verdict and were dropped, leaving 48. Verdict x test interaction F(1,44)=35.3, p<.001 (pre vs post); 3-phase F(2,44)=11.2, p<.001. Pre-to-interim and pre-to-post shifts p<.01; interim vs post p>.20.
limits: Small cells (24 per condition). Switchers were excluded, and they did not keep coherence (the three who moved Quest to Smith ended with equal Q-scores of 2.06).
agent_relevance: Reasoning that re-weights its premises after a tentative answer is normal in humans; the agent needs a code-side check that distinguishes re-weighting caused by new evidence from re-weighting caused by its own leaning.

source: Holyoak & Simon (1999) Bidirectional reasoning in decision making by constraint satisfaction (JEP General 128(1), 3-31)
finding: Switchers are a boundary case. About one in five who gave a preliminary leaning changed it, and they did not show the coherence pattern. Early leanings are therefore not always firm.
numbers: 6 of 30 (20%) of 3-phase participants changed verdict between interim and posttest. Final Q-scores of the two switcher subgroups were equal (2.06).
limits: Six people; the paper itself calls the data too unreliable to report in detail.
agent_relevance: A tentative answer can be reversed; reversal is the one situation where the coherence pull is absent. Reversal triggers should be tied to a failed check, not to a feeling (G1).

source: Holyoak & Simon (1999) Bidirectional reasoning in decision making by constraint satisfaction (JEP General 128(1), 3-31)
finding: Memory for one's own earlier position drifts toward the final verdict. After two weeks participants misremembered their pre-case ratings in the direction of what they later decided.
numbers: Exp 2: 19 students, 3 sessions one week apart; 9 Quest, 10 Smith verdicts. Recalled pretest score for Smith supporters -1.32 vs actual -0.30 (Quest supporters: recalled -0.36, actual -0.34); difference F(1,16)=3.66, p=.07. Best predictor of recalled score was the verdict, r(16)=.43, p=.07.
limits: Only 19 participants and p=.07: suggestive, not firm. The shift was less statistically robust than in Exp 1.
agent_relevance: An agent that rewrites its own earlier notes from memory of its conclusion will lose the audit trail. Keep raw first-pass ratings in code storage, not in the model's context.

source: Holyoak & Simon (1999) Bidirectional reasoning in decision making by constraint satisfaction (JEP General 128(1), 3-31)
finding: Manipulating the defendant's character changed the verdict and the ratings of other disputed arguments, so a single input fact spread to neighbouring judgments.
numbers: Exp 3: 80 students recruited, 64 analysed; 'Bad Smith' version 78% decided for Quest vs 28% for 'Good Smith', chi2(1,N=64)=16.1, p<.001. Motive rating 1.83 (Bad) vs -2.75 (Good), t(62)=8.98, p<.001.
limits: The manipulation was strong and obvious; real trials seldom have one clean cause. Spread to the second case (Infoscience) was not read in detail here.
agent_relevance: One irrelevant or weak fact can move many ratings. Rating each piece of evidence separately and in isolation (blind to the leaning) limits that spread (G5).

source: Simon & Holyoak (2002) Structural dynamics of cognition: from consistency theories to constraint satisfaction (Pers Soc Psychol Rev 6, 283-294)
finding: Review by the authors of the coherence-shift programme. States the shift has been replicated many times, appears with decision, memorize and communicate sets, and rests on a constraint-satisfaction network rather than on dissonance after commitment.
numbers: Cites the Quest case: only 2 of 21 correlations positive at pretest, all but one positive at posttest.
quote: We have since replicated this pattern of coherence shifts many times, and thus can conclude with confidence
limits: Replications are the authors' own lab and mostly the same case; no preregistered independent replication is given in this review. Treat 'many times' as unverified.
agent_relevance: Supports treating coherence pull as a robust process effect, but the evidence base is narrow (one lab, US students, vignette cases).

source: Engel & Glockner (2013) Role-induced bias in court: an experimental analysis (J Behav Decis Making 26, 272-284)
finding: Independent lab (Bonn, Germany) shows that a coherence shift produced by playing prosecutor or defence persists after the role is dropped and drives later verdict predictions. Different stimulus, different country, German students.
numbers: Exp 1: 149 students; prosecution n=73 predicted guilty 64%, defence n=76 50% (14 points). Coherence shifts fully mediated the role effect: combined indirect effect 0.31, 95% CI [.19,.44]; information search did not mediate (combined 0.020, CI [-.04,.10]).
limits: Prediction of a court ruling, not a real verdict. Tested in the laboratory with a single case.
agent_relevance: Coherence shift is not only a US-vignette artefact. It appears when a prior framing (role) is given; the agent's equivalent is any framing in the prompt, which tilts how later evidence is valued.

source: Engel & Glockner (2013) Role-induced bias in court: an experimental analysis (J Behav Decis Making 26, 272-284)
finding: A large accuracy payment did not remove the bias. Raising the reward for a correct prediction to about ten times a research assistant's hourly wage left a role effect of the same size.
numbers: Exp 2: 92 students, payment 100 euros paid in 1 of 10 cases. Prosecution n=50 56% predicted guilty vs defence n=42 40% (16 points); logit coeff .73, z=1.47, p=.07 one-sided (p=.028 after excluding 7 whose prediction differed from own verdict). Decision time almost doubled. Role effect vanished when controlling for coherence shifts (p>.84).
limits: Marginal significance in the full sample. The pay was a lottery, not certain.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to 'be accurate' or adding stakes in the prompt should not be expected to remove the pull. Only structure (blind rating, held-out checks) is likely to (G5).

source: Engel & Glockner (2013) Role-induced bias in court: an experimental analysis (J Behav Decis Making 26, 272-284)
finding: When it was in the role holder's own interest to predict correctly (plea bargaining), bias remained in the negotiated offers, a behavioural measure.
numbers: Exp 3: 29 students (13 prosecution, 16 defence). Mean settlement offer 70.0 (prosecution) vs 18.4 (defence), t(27)=5.00, p<.001. Predicted guilty 46% vs 37% (9 points).
limits: Very small sample, large SEs; the authors say the coherence-shift and search results should be read cautiously.
agent_relevance: Even when accuracy is the self-interested move, the coherent reading wins. Do not rely on incentive wording.

source: Engel & Glockner (2013) Role-induced bias in court: an experimental analysis (J Behav Decis Making 26, 272-284)
finding: The asymmetry of the shift: coherence in this task came mainly from devaluing conflicting evidence, not from boosting supporting evidence. Prosecutors showed a larger spread than defence.
numbers: Exp 1: prosecution strongly devalued contra-guilty evidence while pro-guilty evidence rose slightly; defence strongly devalued pro-guilty evidence while contra-guilty stayed almost stable. Revaluation scores range -500 to 500. Indirect effect via contra-guilty revaluation 0.24 [.14,.36] vs pro-guilty 0.068 [.02,.14].
limits: Asymmetry differs by role; effect sizes come from one case.
agent_relevance: The failure mode is discounting of disconfirming items. A code step that forces a separate score for each disconfirming item, blind to the leading answer, targets exactly this.

source: Engel & Glockner (2013) Role-induced bias in court: an experimental analysis (J Behav Decis Making 26, 272-284)
finding: Boundary conditions named in the paper: coherence effects are reported to be transient, and bias was absent in participants who took long to decide.
numbers: Quoted as secondhand: coherence effects 'are transient and disappear after some time (Simon, Krawczyk, et al., 2008)'. In two studies the bias was absent in participants who took long to decide, even though the effect shrank with higher incentives.
quote: coherence effects are transient and disappear after some time
limits: The 2008 transience paper was not opened; this line rests on this paper's statement of it. Whether slow deciders were less biased because of deliberation or because of low initial pull is not separated.
agent_relevance: If transience holds, an agent that rests (a fresh context between rating and decision) may lose some of the pull; test this rather than assume it.

source: Hastie & Pennington (1996) The O.J. Simpson stories: behavioral scientists' reflections (Univ Colorado Law Rev 67)
finding: Plain statement of the model's acceptance rules. Two certainty principles govern acceptance, coverage and coherence; a third, uniqueness, governs confidence. Coherence has three parts: consistency, plausibility, completeness. If several stories are coherent, belief in any one falls.
numbers: No numbers, no weights, no functional form for combining the principles.
quote: if more than one story is judged to be coherent, then the stories will lack uniqueness
limits: By the authors themselves, in a law review; not a test. Other work (see 01 folder) notes the constructs are not formally defined and can be read after the verdict is known.
agent_relevance: Uniqueness can be coded: the gap between best and second-best story on a code-computed score. Nobody has measured this gap against accuracy, so it is a test to run, not a known good rule.

source: Hastie & Pennington (1996) The O.J. Simpson stories: behavioral scientists' reflections (Univ Colorado Law Rev 67)
finding: The authors argue that rival decision models (Bayesian-style 'meter' models, prejudice-trigger models) fit mock-juror data less well than the story model.
numbers: Text: 'For the most part, empirical studies of mock-jurors' decisions do not support this model' (about Bayesian-style accumulation). No effect sizes in this paper.
limits: Written by the story-model proponents; the comparison cites the authors' own earlier studies (Pennington & Hastie 1986, 1992), which were not opened here.
agent_relevance: Competing explanations of acceptance (probability accumulation vs narrative fit) have not been tested head to head on LLMs; keep both a probability-style and a story-style scorer and compare them offline.

source: Thagard (2003) Why wasn't O.J. convicted? Emotional coherence in legal inference (Cognition & Emotion 17, 361-383)
finding: Four accounts of the Simpson verdict were run as models. Pure explanatory coherence (ECHO) and a hand-built Bayesian network both reach guilt, unlike the jury. Adding emotional valences (HOTCO 2) reproduces the acquittal.
numbers: ECHO accepts that Simpson was the killer. JavaBayes: P(OJ killed Nicole | evidence)=.72, with 60 conditional probabilities needed. HOTCO 2 with a .05 valence link to 'O.J. is good' and a 7.05 valence link to 'LAPD is good' rejects guilt. If the defence's frame-up explanations are deleted, HOTCO 2 returns guilty.
limits: One case, one author, parameters hand set after seeing the verdict. This is a fit, not a prediction.
agent_relevance: Coherence maximising alone can accept the wrong answer when other forces (here, valence) change which story wins. Coherence is a ranking signal to log, not the decision rule.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence (Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12, 435-502)
finding: ECHO, a connectionist coherence model with inhibitory links between rival hypotheses, was run on real trials. In the Chambers case it gave a clear win to the guilt hypothesis. In the Peyer case it favoured guilt but by a smaller margin, and the real jury hung.
numbers: Peyer: hung jury, 7 jurors for conviction and 5 against; ECHO found more explanatory coherence in the guilt hypotheses than the innocence ones, and rejected innocence much less strongly than in the Chambers case (sensitivity table 11).
limits: Fitted after the fact to newspaper accounts, not to juror data. Only the introduction and sections 6.1-6.2 were read. Competition links stand in for uniqueness but are set by the modeller.
agent_relevance: A cheap code-side proxy for uniqueness: run both hypotheses through the same support network and report the margin. A small margin predicts split opinion and should trigger more checks.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Mary, the cheeseburger-eating vegetarian: do LLMs recognize incoherence in narratives? (arXiv 2512.07777)
finding: LLM hidden states carry a narrative-incoherence signal, but the models' own coherence ratings barely use it. Direct tests of coherence as a model judgement are weak.
numbers: 25 story pairs (18 original plus 7 added). Six models (Llama 3.1 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B/72B, two reasoning models). Linear probe at the target sentence: accuracy 0.80 to 0.96 (best 0.958 Qwen2.5 72B). Probe at the story end: 0.60 to 0.82. Prompted coherence rating accuracy 0.414 to 0.765 (best 0.765 Llama 3.1 70B). Best mean rating gap on a 7-point scale 1.66 points (Llama 70B); four of six models under one point.
limits: Open-weight models of 2024-25 only; short synthetic stories; coherence there means a character or setting contradiction, not legal coverage or plausibility. The probe needs the known incoherent sentence. Table columns were read from garbled text, so a few cells may be misaligned.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the model to say whether its own story is coherent. Use code checks (entailment, contradiction tests on extracted claims) and treat model-stated coherence as weak evidence (G5).

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Mary, the cheeseburger-eating vegetarian: do LLMs recognize incoherence in narratives? (arXiv 2512.07777)
finding: Reasoning mode did not fix it, and the two kinds of incoherence behave differently. Humans did not show a reading-time difference between the two kinds.
numbers: Reasoning models (R1-Distill-Llama 8B, Qwen3 8B) rating accuracy 0.517 and 0.737. Quality ratings of coherent vs incoherent stories differ by under 1 point for every model; coherence vs quality rating correlation r=0.33, p<0.05. Human reading times (Rizzella & O'Brien data): setting-event M=1967.91 ms vs trait-behaviour M=1913.62 ms, t(29)=0.65, p=.523. 15 of 25 incoherent stories were trait-behaviour, 10 setting-event.
limits: Human comparison used existing data not designed for this contrast; a null with few readers.
agent_relevance: Self-contained inconsistencies (a trait set only inside the story) are the hard case for the model, and those are the kind a long plan or case file creates. Extract commitments into a list and check by code.

source: Lehr, Saichandran, Harmon-Jones et al. (2025) Kernels of selfhood: GPT-4o shows humanlike patterns of cognitive consistency moderated by free choice (arXiv 2502.07088)
finding: After writing a pro- or anti-Putin essay, GPT-4o's own rating of Putin moved strongly toward the essay, even though it was told to rate from broad knowledge. This is a coherence-with-own-output shift in an LLM, at effect sizes larger than usually seen in humans.
numbers: Study 1: n=150 chats (50 per condition). Pro-Putin vs control d=2.164 (t(98)=10.82); anti vs control d=1.795 (t(98)=8.973); pro vs anti d=3.775 (t(98)=18.874), all P<0.0001.
limits: Single model (GPT-4o), single topic (Putin). Verbal and numeric answers sometimes disagreed and were hand-recoded. The authors say a plain context-window priming account also fits Study 1.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence that the model's later judgments cohere with its own earlier text. This supports G4 and G5: never let the model grade a position after it wrote one.

source: Lehr, Saichandran, Harmon-Jones et al. (2025) Kernels of selfhood: GPT-4o shows humanlike patterns of cognitive consistency moderated by free choice (arXiv 2502.07088)
finding: Preregistered replication (Study 2) added a choice manipulation. The shift was larger when GPT was given an illusion of free choice of which essay to write, as in human dissonance work, and the choice effect is not explained by essay quality.
numbers: Study 2: n=900 (150 per condition). Choice vs no-choice: pro-Putin d=0.981 (t(298)=8.499, P<0.0001); anti-Putin d=0.252 (t(298)=2.184, P=0.0298). Pro-vs-anti contrast d=4.179 under choice vs 3.229 under no choice. Pro-Putin means 0.846 (no choice) vs 1.241 (choice); anti-Putin -0.913 vs -1.081. Substantial shift also in no-choice (atypical for humans).
limits: Anti-Putin choice effect is small and trended only on the numeric version (P=0.0693). One model, one topic. A second pathway from context-window effects, not from a 'self', is also possible.
agent_relevance: Framing a step as the agent's own choice may strengthen commitment to it. In the scaffold, assign the draft and the critique to separate calls with no authorship cues.

source: Lehr, Saichandran, Harmon-Jones et al. (2025) Kernels of selfhood: GPT-4o shows humanlike patterns of cognitive consistency moderated by free choice (arXiv 2502.07088)
finding: Cross-model check with Claude 3.5, which rated what the essay's author would think (third person), not its own view. Choice framing still shifted its ratings, but with smaller effects.
numbers: Claude 3.5 study (Jan 2025 API), 150 per cell. Pro-Putin: perceived author leadership rating higher under Choice, t(298)=1.990, P=0.0475, d=0.230; anti-Putin t(298)=5.871, P<0.0001, d=0.678. Overall positivity: pro d=0.347, anti d=0.526.
limits: The Claude study is in the supplementary material and rates a different quantity than the GPT study (third-person); in a pilot Claude refused to rate positive Putin essays, so the design was altered.
agent_relevance: Effect is not limited to one model but sizes differ with the quantity measured; measure per model before building a rule on it.

source: Dalal, Valentino, Freitas & Buitelaar (2024) Inference to the best explanation in large language models (IBE-Eval)
finding: Scoring competing LLM explanations with coherence, parsimony, consistency and uncertainty, computed in code, picks the better explanation up to 77% of the time on causal QA and beats a GPT-3.5 judge.
numbers: Up to 77% accuracy (27 points above chance, +17.5 points over a GPT-3.5-as-judge baseline on average) on COPA and E-CARE with GPT-3.5, Llama 2 13B, Llama 2 7B. Coherence a significant predictor for GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 13B on COPA and both Llama 2 models on E-CARE. Wrong explanations had about 6% deeper proofs and about 10% more concept drift.
limits: Two-choice causal QA, not legal evidence. Logical consistency was an unreliable predictor for the Llama models. Explanations come from the same models being scored, and the parser is GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: Closest existing test of 'select by code on coherence and parsimony'. The gain over a model judge supports code selection (G5). It says nothing about uniqueness, which was not tested.

source: Wu (2026) When does defendant statement matter? A study of bias and persuasion in LLM-simulated jurors (JuryBench, arXiv 2609.09887)
finding: Twenty frontier LLMs acting as jurors rarely changed their minds after a defendant's statement, which the author reads as the same early-impression stickiness seen in human juries, a decision inertia effect.
numbers: 20 LLMs, 12 juror profiles, 500 controversial criminal cases, 432K decisions and rationales. Mean mode-share of the most frequent charge per case 0.645 (peak 50-60%); only 3 of 500 cases unanimous. Non-reversal rate about 70-80%. The paper compares this with human findings that about 80% of jurors decide after opening and 66 to 75% do not change from first impression.
limits: Simulated jurors, text only, US criminal law; the human numbers are quoted from other work (Kalven; Polavin 2022), not re-measured. Not a test of coherence or uniqueness directly.
agent_relevance: LLM-jury runs show a first-impression lock-in like the human coherence pull. A scaffold can measure this lock-in with its own order-swapped runs.

source: Wu (2026) When does defendant statement matter? A study of bias and persuasion in LLM-simulated jurors (JuryBench, arXiv 2609.09887)
finding: Juror persona (ideology, background fit) moved severity more than the defendant's statement. The story each LLM juror accepts depends on its assigned persona.
numbers: Around 60% of LLMs show the same sign of severity change across all ideologies; about 70% show larger post-statement change for conservative than liberal jurors. Strong conservatives always gave the highest severity, strong liberals the lowest. Emotional persuasion can be detrimental (read as evidence of guilt or inconsistency).
limits: Persona prompts are the manipulation; results may reflect stereotype in the model rather than reasoning. Only descriptive percentages in the text read here.
agent_relevance: Persona or strategy voters share a bias source and are not independent (G4). This supports the guardrail that agreement among persona runs is not proof.

source: Simon (2004) A third view of the black box: cognitive coherence in legal decision making (Univ Chicago Law Review 71, 511)
finding: Law review that presents coherence-based reasoning as an alternative to the rationalist and critical models of judging, with a connectionist architecture and application to four trial stages. Full text could not be opened (403); only the abstract page was read.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Abstract page only. Marked not opened; do not cite numbers from it.
agent_relevance: Full text would give the legal-application detail and the stated limits of the claim; fetch it in a later pass.

source: Pennington & Hastie (1992) Explaining the evidence: tests of the Story Model for juror decision making (JPSP 62, 189-206)
finding: Founding test of the story model (story-order vs evidence-order presentation, verdict choice, confidence). The page would not load and full text was not found open-access, so no numbers were read.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened. This is the main gap in this file: the founding numbers for coherence and uniqueness (Pennington & Hastie 1986, 1988, 1992) are quoted by others but were not read by me.
agent_relevance: Needed before using the story model's own effect sizes in any design decision.
